scenes.heading: Methods & Receivers
scenes.narration: Let's dig into Methods and Receivers, where one small choice decides whether your updates actually persist.

scenes.heading: A method is a function with a receiver
items: The receiver binds the method to a type
Value receiver operates on a copy
Pointer receiver operates on the original
scenes.narration: A method is just a function with a special receiver argument, written in parentheses before the name, binding the method to a type. The single most important decision is the receiver kind. A value receiver operates on a copy of the value, so mutations don't persist. A pointer receiver operates on the original through its address, so mutations do persist. Get this right and methods feel obvious; get it wrong and your updates silently vanish.

scenes.heading: What happens on a pointer-receiver call
steps: Inc needs a *Counter, but c is a value
c is addressable, so Go rewrites c.Inc() as (&c).Inc()
c.n++ writes to the original's memory
scenes.narration: Trace a pointer-receiver call. Inc is declared on star Counter, but you call it on a plain Counter value. Because that value is addressable, the compiler quietly rewrites c dot Inc into ampersand c dot Inc, taking the address for you. The method receives an eight-byte pointer to the real Counter, not a copy of its fields. Inside, c dot n plus plus writes to the original's memory, so when control returns, the caller sees the increment.

scenes.heading: Value vs pointer receiver, side by side
scenes.narration: Here the two receivers sit side by side. IncCopy has a value receiver, so it bumps a throwaway copy and the change is lost; after calling it, n is still zero. IncReal has a pointer receiver, so the increment writes to the real Counter and after the call n is one. This is the single most important behavior to internalize: value receivers read, pointer receivers mutate.

scenes.text: Only *T's method set has pointer-receiver methods, so pick one receiver kind per type and stay consistent.
scenes.narration: One consequence matters for interfaces: the method set of T holds only value-receiver methods, while star T holds both. So if any method needs a pointer receiver, only star T satisfies an interface requiring it. The practical rule is simple: once a type has mutable state, make all of its methods pointer receivers so behavior and interface satisfaction stay predictable.
